newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch closing debt market report.
newsitem.headline: Dutch closing debt market report.

text.p: Dutch bonds closed with heavy losses, with dealers attributing most of the damage to a weaker U.S. Treasury bond market.
Prices had already begun to crumble after the Bundesbank left interest rates unchanged, even though this was expected.
They fell further later in the session when technical selling and nervousness ahead of tomorrow's U.S. employment data drove U.S. Treasury bond prices lower.
Dealers said Dutch institutions continued to be attracted by medium maturities of around five years, but that the recent wave of shortening trades had made this segment relatively expensive.
"The five-to-ten year spread has steepened to 100 basis points from around 90 just over a week ago. Five year Dutch paper also looks expensive against Germany," said one dealer.
The Dutch September 2001 bond was currently yielding some eight basis points below its German equivalent, having traded at the same yield a fortnight ago, he added.
Dealers said some money was gradually drifting back into the 10-year segment of the Dutch curve, prompted by a feeling that the long end had been oversold.
Some Dutch investors had sold bunds and bought back guilders, they said, prompted by a recent narrowing of the 10-year Dutch-German yield spread.
Dutch 10-year bonds were yielding just three or four basis points below their German equivalents earlier this week compared with 12 to 13 basis points below a month ago.
By the close of trade on Thursday the spread had widened to six basis points again.

Much of the narrowing in the yield differential has been attributed to a widening inflation gap in Germany's favour, with preliminary West German November inflation reported at 1.4 percent and Dutch November inflation estimated at 2.4 percent.
But dealers said attention was likely to refocus soon on the Dutch state's unusually low bond issuance in 1997, causing the spread to widen again in the Netherlands' favour.
"I would expect the Dutch-German spread to get back around to 10 basis points," said one dealer.
